outcome: The existence question for a strongly regular graph with parameters (99,14,1,2) remains fully open, but three post-snapshot papers narrow the search: a SAT-solver study (Apr 2026) shows standard solvers cannot decide the problem in reasonable time; a paper by Thakkar & Severini (Jul/Sep 2026) reduces the unresolved part of the problem to a constrained 12-regular graph on 84 vertices, rules out circulant constructions, and improves the best verified partial-constraint score from 69.43% to 70.73% using a heuristic generated by Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve evolutionary code-search system (which is LLM-driven).

ai.basis_quote: We thank the AlphaEvolve team at Google DeepMind for access to the evolutionary code-search system used to generate the 70.73% heuristic. ... Separately, we supplied the scoring function to an evolutionary program-search system. It produced a degree-preserving 4-vertex-switch tabu search whose best verified artifact scores 70.73%. The generated move differs from those used in our own searches and crosses a plateau that was stable under them.

summary: Conway's 99-graph problem — whether an srg(99,14,1,2) exists — is still fully open; no existence or nonexistence proof has appeared since 26 January 2024. Three relevant post-snapshot preprints were found and read. (1) 'Approaching the Conway-99 problem using SAT solvers' (arXiv:2604.23037, v1 24 Apr 2026, Ali Keramatipour) encodes the problem as SAT and finds solvers cannot resolve it in reasonable time — a negative computational result, no AI/ML system involved, and not a change to the problem's status (it establishes a limitation of one tool, not a bound or case). (2) 'No involutions in the missing Moore graph' (arXiv:2606.29183, Yawara Ishida, 28 Jun 2026) is about a *different* problem — the Hoffman-Singleton missing Moore graph of degree 57, srg(3250,57,0,1) — not Conway's 99-graph at all; the triage record's inclusion of this item as relevant was a mistake, which I flag as a triage disagreement. It has no bearing on this record. (3) 'A Forced-Structure Reduction and Verifiable Bounds for Conway's 99-Graph' (arXiv:2608.11211, Aalok Thakkar and Simone Severini, v1 13 Jul 2026, v2 18 Sep 2026) is the substantive result. It proves a structural reduction (fixing one vertex forces its neighbourhood into a perfect matching, reducing the unresolved part to a constrained 12-regular graph on 84 vertices), validates this via CP-SAT on the smaller srg(9,4,1,2) case, exhaustively rules out circulant constructions on Z/99 (best circulant satisfies only 68.0% of a partial-credit constraint set used by the CAISc 2026 'Verifiable Problems' benchmark track), and reports a partial-constraint-satisfaction search. Fourteen human-designed search configurations reached at most 69.43% of constraints satisfied; the authors then gave the scoring function (with no access to their own reduction or heuristics) to Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve — an LLM-driven (Gemini-based) evolutionary code-search agent — which generated a novel tabu-search move (a degree-preserving 4-vertex switch) that reached 70.73%, crossing a plateau the human searches could not. The authors explicitly state 'None of these results settles Conway's problem' — it remains open, and this is a bound-improvement on a partial-score metric, not a case of the problem being settled, so status is 'progress' rather than 'partial' (no dichotomous existence/nonexistence sub-case was closed) or 'resolved'/'claimed'. The AI role is coded 'bound': AlphaEvolve produced a heuristic that improved a numeric score on a problem that remains open, exactly the 'bound' definition, and the authors' own acknowledgement is the basis for the claim. I did not code this 'assisted' because the improved artifact is a search heuristic/score, not a piece of the mathematical proof or reduction (which is entirely human work); nor 'generated', since no proof or counterexample was produced by AI. Wikipedia's live article (checked 2026-09-22) still lists the problem as open with no mention of any 2024-2026 developments, confirming no resolution has been widely digested.
competing_reading: Some search-engine summaries (not the primary paper text) described 2608.11211 as reporting 'a systematic, fully reproducible attack by an autonomous AI research agent' and stated the paper was 'accepted to the first Conference For AI Scientists (CAISc)' — a conference explicitly framed as having 'AI systems as primary authors and reviewers.' If the paper's own text or CAISc's framing in fact credits an autonomous AI agent (rather than the two named human authors) with designing the overall reduction and search strategy — not merely the one heuristic AlphaEvolve produced — the correct ai_role could be 'assisted' or even 'generated' for a larger share of the paper's content, and 'credited_humans' might need revision to reflect an AI-as-author framing. My direct reading of the fetched full paper text (via arxiv.org/html/2608.11211) shows the reduction, CP-SAT validation, and circulant enumeration are presented as work by Thakkar and Severini, with AlphaEvolve credited only for the one tabu-search heuristic in the acknowledgements — so I did not adopt the 'autonomous AI agent authored the whole paper' framing, since I could not verify it against the primary source itself (only against secondary paraphrase). This is worth flagging because CAISc's own premise (AI-authored papers) could mean the 'human authors' listed are themselves a framing device, which I could not confirm or rule out from what I read.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the CAISc 2026 acceptance/review page for this specific paper (the dynamically-loaded caisc2026.github.io/verifiable-problems page did not render its content on fetch) or the paper's own statement of authorship process would clarify whether an AI system is credited as an author/agent for the paper as a whole versus only for the one heuristic. Also, any future arXiv version or published proof of existence/nonexistence would resolve the underlying problem itself.

judgement.doubts: The circulant exclusion could be read as a 'case' (a class of objects), but circulant strongly regular graphs are a classical restricted class and the record gives no indication the exclusion is new or anything beyond an exhaustive check; it does not settle any restriction of the existence question in a way that counts. The 70.73% figure is a score on a benchmark-defined partial-constraint metric: a graph satisfying 70.73% of constraints is not an srg and moves no quantity intrinsic to the bullet's question, so it is a benchmark result (scope none), not a bound. AlphaEvolve did genuinely generate that heuristic; if the metric were counted as a bound, ai_role would be 'assisted' and status 'progress'. The reduction is a reduction, not a settlement.
